General Handle Description

    The reason the SPECTRE Handle was created was to provide the Bally Arcade with a true joystick input device.  Since this required the use of two handle ports, we also had available 5 switch contacts per port.  So we used the 10 switches to add a keypad.  As an extra, we added the pinball buttons, (which duplicate the #5 and #0 keys).

    To get the joystick to correspond to a left to right movement from the KN(X) function in your programs you will need to used a negative sign.  This was done so that the handle will work with the absolute machine addressing.

    The accuracy of the joystick is +/- 2 pixels. This is because of the way the Bally decodes analog to digital signals and must be dealt with using software debouncing.

    We have found that some cartridges can use the SPECTRE Handle.  For example it was designed to work with Bally Pin by using the two pinball buttons for the flipper, and the #7 key of the keypad to launch the ball.  You can just pass the handle to the next player when it is their turn.

    By experimentation you can see if the SPECTRE Handle will work with the other cartridges you have.


Page 1

------------------------------------------------------------

    The SPECTRE Handle is a new, versatile control handle to be used with the Bally or Astro Arcade.  It provides an X-Y analog joystick, an 11-key keypad, and two pinball style flipper buttons.  All these functions are accessible from BASIC or machine language programs, as well as the cartridge programs.

    The SPECTRE Handle uses two standard handle cords, which plug into two handle inputs on the Arcade.  The handle inputs you use depends on the program you are running, and should be specified in that program's documentation.  For the enclosed examples, use input one for the right cord, and input two for the left cord (looking at the Handle from the back).

    A maximum of two SPECTRE handles may be plugged into the arcade at one time.

    In order to utilize the Handle in your basic programs, the following inputs are provided if the Handle is plugged in as above.

SPECTRE Handle Values  BASIC Value

X Joystick Value       KN(1)= -128 to 127
Y Joystick Value       KN(2)= -128 to 127
Left Button Value      TR(1)= 1
Right Button Value     TR(2)= 1
Keypad - 0             TR(2)= 1
Keypad - 1             JX(2)= -1
Keypad - 2             JY(1)= -1
keypad - 3             JY(2)= -1
Keypad - 4             JX(1)= -1
Keypad - 5             TR(1)= 1
Keypad - 6             JX(1)= 1
Keypad - 7             JY(2)= 1
Keypad - 8             JY(1)= 1
Keypad - 9             JX(2)= 1
Keypad - S             Future Expansion


Port access Value

&(28)= 0 to 255
&(29)= 0 to 255
All functions with a (1) [handle port #1] after them are mapped to port &(16) All functions with a (2) [handle port #2] after them are mapped to port &(17)

Byte - 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
                 T R L D U

[T = Trigger, R = Joystick pushed right, L = Joystick pushed left, D = Joystick pulled backwards, U = Joystick pushed forward]

The value for the port depends on which bits are set in the byte.
The switch banks return a one-byte value which can be stored directly in a variable.  The bits set by the switches determine the value returned.  When using port values to determine switch settings you must look at the bits that are set in the byte returned.

EXAMPLE 1 - [A = &(16)]: if &(16) equals 18 this would mean the trigger is pulled and the joystick is pulled back for handle port #1. i.e. Trigger(T) = 16 and the joystick is pulled back. (D) = 2 : 16 + 2 = 18 and therefore the variable A will equal 18.

EXAMPLE 2 - If you let variable B= &(17) and &(17) equals 10, then this would mean that handle port #2 would give this value if handle #2 had the Joystick pushed to the right(R) and pulled backward(D) at the same time, i.e. 8+2=10.

Keys 8, 2, 4, 6, 5, are the up, down, left, right, and trigger functions of the Bally handle #1.

Keys 7, 3, 1, 9, 6, are the up, down, left, right, and trigger functions of the Bally handle #2.

Maintenance

    Maintenance - The SPECTRE Handle was designed to require a minimum of user maintenance.  It may be required that with time the pinball button contacts will need to be cleaned.  When you need to clean the contacts, remove the four corner screws, and carefully lift the lid, (DO NOT PULL ON THE WIRES).  On both sides you will see the pinball housings holding the leaf contact switches.  Where the leaf switches make contact you will see small copper rivets.  By using fine sandpaper or a fingernail emery board, gently clean the oxidation off these contacts.  Be careful not to bend the leaf contacts.  If you do bend a leaf contact, use a pair of needle nose pliers to carefully straighten it.

    It may also be necessary to clean the joystick potentiometers.  This may be done by spraying contact cleaner into the potentiometers.  Make sure that the contact cleaner you use is safe for cleaning potentiometers, and that you follow the directions to prevent damage to the joystick

    The keypad should not require any maintenance.

Program Documentation

We have provided some simple programs with the handle to help show its operations.

    'Animated Box' - This simple short program shows how the joystick can be used with the Bally Basic graphic commands to produce effects not achievable with the normal Ball handle.  Move the joystick around to see a box vary in size on the screen.

    'Get the Box' - This program is to help you to adapt to using the joystick.  You will be asked for a difficulty level; 1 is the hardest with larger numbers being easier (use values less than 15).  Use the Arcade keypad to enter values.  The object will be to move the blinkinq dot (representing where the joystick is) to hit the solid box.  The faster you can hit the boxes, the lower and better your score.  You will see your score after you have hit 20 boxes.  To start, press the left button and be ready to move the blinking box with the joystick.  After you have seen your score, press any key on the Arcade keypad to start again.

    'Keypad Game' - This is a simple program to show you how to use the port values to access the SPECTRE keypad.  It compares what key is pressed to what square is selected.  Press the left button to start and be ready to press the key that corresponds to the square with a box in it.  The scoring is similar to 'Get the Box.'  The lower the score the better.

These are simple programs to help you understand how to use the handle for your own programs.

Accurately Dumping an Astrocade ROM
-----------------------------------
April 23, 2007
By Adam Trionfo


I want to archive the unarchived 3159 Bally Arcade ROM, so I spent a few hours today verifying how to dump the Bally Astrocade ROM to tape.  This may prove helpful, as this provides a relatively easy process to dump your Astrocade's ROM.

The first step that I took was to hookup the Astrocade to the microphone input of my computer.  Then, while recording, I used

this command in AstroBASIC to dump the 8K ROM:

:PRINT %(0),4096

This command dumped 8193 bytes to tape (including the one byte checksum).  Technically I don't use tapes anymore: I use my computer (in this case an older laptop (circa 2001 or so) that is running Windows XP).

After I dumped the program to my computer as a WAV file, I used the Ballybin 2.0 beta to create a BML file.  I tried SO many variations of Ballybin to create a plain 8192 byte binary file so that I wouldn't have to go through the following time-consuming process, but I could not figure-out how to get it done (it may not even be possible).  In the end I avoided the plain binary file and I used this command to create a BML file:

ballybin -v2 -i1 astrocadeROM.wav

This created a BML file that read the WAV file as plain data (i.e. not as a BASIC file- which would have read only every other byte as data).  With the BML file completed, I aimed to delete all of the extraneous BML syntax to leave only the binary data (though, for now, in ASCII format).

I used Word to delete the data surrounding the ROM data.  I used ALT-right-click to delete the data to the left and right of the binary data that I wanted to keep.  (ALT-right-clicking to clean-up a file is one of Word's handiest features.  If you don't use it, then I HIGHLY recommend that you try it out!)

After I had the 8192 of ASCII bytes in Word, I put it into the clipboard and then pasted it into a hex editor called WinHex.  This hex editor allows you to choose seventeen different ways to import data: I chose ASCII-Hex.  Win-Hex created an 8192-byte binary file which I then saved for the next step: comparison.

Using a file compare program called HowDif I compared my new 8192-byte file to the already dumped 3159 Astrocade ROM.  I crossed my fingers that they would be byte-for-byte identical (they had to be, otherwise something was wrong).  The two files were byte-for-byte identical!  The process had worked!

I proved to myself that I could accurately dump the Astrocade ROM using only software.  Now I have to get my non-workingpotential-3164-Astrocade working so that I can dump the ROM and see if it differs from the already archived White Astrocade ROM and the 3159 Astrocade ROM.

After trying the 3159/3164 ROM test and coming up with an already archived ROM, I began to wonder, how many people have tried this test?  It's VERY easy to do, and if you run the test and it turns out that you DO have the unarchived 3164 ROM, then it's a simple matter of recording the ROM to the computer just as you would record any audio.  You wouldn't even have to archive the ROM yourself, that is, you could just send along the RAW WAV file as you recorded it.  There would be no need to learn to use the archive utilities.

The test takes just about five minutes to run and it is VERY simple to do (just type in one line of BASIC and then press GO).  Anyone that is interested in running the test on their Astrocade, please try it!

Here is a summary of how to run the test:

In AstroBASIC type the following program from the ARCADIAN newsletter (Vol. 5, No. 3, Pg. 49, Jan. 14, 1983):

CLEAR;%(19904)=-43;%(19906)=12341;%(19908)=27651;%(19910)=3164;%(19912)=-
13871;CALL19904

After entering this program (which takes up four lines of text), press GO.  The program will run without the need to type run because you're typing it in immediate mode.  The results of this program are that on the screen, in large letters, will be either the word OVER or the words GAME OVER.  If your results are the words GAME OVER, then you have the ROM that has not yet been archived!

If you would like to know more about this, then read the full (short) article here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/identify_bally_rom.pdf

One advantage of reading the article is that there are a couple of screenshots to show you what to expect to see on the screen when you type the program and after the program runs.

After Adam linked to the Sprectre joystick description, I realized
that it wasn't doing anything completely unique, just putting the
standard player 1 and 2 joysticks into a new interface.  With this, I
suspected, and confirmed, that you can play ICBM Attack in MESS--you
just have to map the controls correctly!

I don't see any instructions, but from what I can tell, ICBM Attack
has 5 controls.  The player 1 knob moves the crosshairs left and
right.  The player 2 knob moves the crosshair up and down.  The player
1 trigger fires from the center outpost to the crosshairs.  Pushing
left on the player 1 joystick fires from the left outpost, and pushing
righ fires from the right outpost.

So, any mapping of these should work, but to really be playable, I'd
recommend a dual analog PC joystick.  I used an XBox 360 controller,
which plugs right into the USB port.  I mapped the player 1 knob to
the left analog stick, the player 2 knob to the right analog stick,
and the trigger, left, and right to three shoulder buttons.  When
mapping the controls, it is very important that you go to analog
options and set the autocenter speed on both knobs to 0--otherwise the
crosshairs will automatically move back to the upper left.  It's
possible to map both knobs to a single analog stick, but I found that
I couldn't reach the lower left when doing this.

Here are a few things to remember.  You have to activate joystick
input in MESS.  There's a checkbox under the controller options.  I've
always had trouble with the new UI, so I uncheck "Use New UI" under
miscellaneous options, then use tab to bring up the menu.  When
starting ICBM Attack, you'll just see a black screen.  Reset the
system to bring up the game.  This is how the actual game worked!

As for gameplay, it's still tricky to get used to.  Try to shoot the
ship from whatever outpost is closest.  You can also shoot the bullets
to keep them from destroying outposts.  If the left, right, or center
outpost is destroyed, you can't shoot from it anymore.  You also have
limited ammo at each outpost.  I've made it to level 2, but no
further; however, I haven't practiced a great deal.

I mentioned before that Spectre controller support was in the bug
reports for MESS.  I imagine this would be an easy fix, since all
you'd really need is a specially labelled controller mapping option.

Actually, it's more the other way around.  My earlier statement about
the CPU running @ 3.58 MHz was from memory, and not referring to the
documentation.  Now that I have, the crystal is 14.31818 MHz, 4x
subcarrier.  This is divided by two by a flip flop (U16)to become 7M
and 7M#, input to the Data chip.  The Data chip divides this by two to
become PX and PX#, used to generate DRAM timing, and again by two to
become PHI and PHI#.    PHI is the clock to the CPU, at 14.31818 MHz
dvided by 8, or 1.789 MHz.

My dad bought one of the first IBM PCs in late 1980 and I ended up starting programming it in BASIC, and later assembler.  After that I moved on to program on the c-64 and Amiga. The emulator works very well for this programming cartridges.  All of the simple programs that I wrote several years ago were done in the MESS emulator before I burned them to EPROM to try them on an actual Astrocade. For some reason people seem to not like EPROM development.  I dont understand why.  If you had to work exclusively with an EPROM cartridge (i.e. no emulator), then I could understand that it might slow you down a little bit, but since most testing would be done on the emulator before making an EPROM cartridge, then this shouldnt be a problem anymore.  Besides, EPROM development was how it was done in the old days-- it could work just as well for you.

You can make an EPROM cartridge VERY easy.  You can get all of the parts from Mike White for ten bucks.  Then you need to add in a low-profile socket.  Solder it together, cut a hole in the bottom on the cartridge for the EPROM to fit through and youre in business.  The cartridge will work for an 8K EPROM, but would need some modification for a 2K or a 4K EPROM.  As for me, I never modified my cartridge: I just always burn an 8K EPROM, even if the program is only a few hundred bytes long.

One method of loading a game written in machine language that I've mentioned in the past, but that hasn't been used very often (certainly not at all since the early eightues), is to load the ML program using AstroBASIC.  This wouldn't give you much memory to work with (perhaps a little over 1K, depending on how much of the screen that you want to take up with code), but you could at least play around with coding the Astrocade a bit -- get some graphics moving around faster than at BASIC's snails pace.

Using this method probably seems that 1K isnt lot to work with, but since you could use the ROM subroutines, youd have a bit of memory to use for your own program.  Youd be limiting your screen height (unless you get creative as to where you store your program in memory, like Super Slope does).  This would also mean that you would be trading off speed and some flexibility for extra bytes of memory, but isnt that always the case?  An advantage of this method is that you can have a nice title screen as the first load of the "tape," and it wont take up any extra RAM.

deems to have been the most significant players.  To do so diminishes the

piecing back together a complete snapshot of a very obscure (but at times
historically significant) portion of computer history.

Paul wrote:
>>
I grew up with the NES and SNES, so the Astrocade and it's kin do seem like dinosaurs after a fashion.
>>

I'm going to be thirty-five this summer, so I SHOULD have grown up with the Atari 2600, but I didn't get one until Christmas of 1982 (I think) when I was ten.  I was very happy with it for about a year or so (I owned six games, though I borrowed carts from friends as it seemed everyone had this system).  My favorite game was Chopper Command, which I got right before getting rid of the system.  I also enjoyed playing Pitfall and flipping Asteroids.  Looking back at that time, I can't believe that I would spend time FLIPPING Asteroids!  That game is too easy (on the levels that I played, anyway).

In sixth grade I saw a Vic-20 at school that someone had brought in for a school project.  This was a REAL computer and I drooled over the ads in the paper for this $99 machine.  At eleven years old I decided to save my money and get one.  It took me over a year, and during that time I was a real miser- I didn't spend a dime; I just had a load of rolled up one-dollar and five-dollar bills that I hid in my bedroom (as if someone was going to steal my money from me).  My mother used to get kind of agitated with me because I wouldn't even spend money on ice cream from the ice cream truck.  If she gave me money, I didn't want to buy ANYTHING; my eyes were set on a computer!  By the time I saved enough money (and with my parents pitching in plenty of dough) I ended up getting a C64 (with disk drive, printer and color TV) instead.  So, I grew up with a C64 and then a C128, and then the NES (which always sort of seemed like a step backward from the C64 (a computer!), but it had the best games-- Mario and Zelda!).

I didn't know about the Astrocade until I started buying classic gaming books in about 1992/3.  It was mentioned more as a computer than a gaming console.  In fact, for many years I believed those books; I thought that the ZGrass would turn up on my next trip to Goodwill or the flea market.  When finally did see an Astrocade at the flea market for a dollar, I snapped it up.  God was that thing trashed; I can't believe that it worked.  It looked like it had been pulled straight out of a dump!  I also had bought BASIC for another dollar from the same guy (without docs or an overlay) and had not IDEA how to use the system.  I worked out how to type using trail and error, and I wrote SUPER short, VERY simple programs using FOR/NEXT loops and other simple "word" commands that I had discovered.  These programs weren't games; they were just a little playing around so that I could get a taste of what the system could do.  I knew that BASIC could save to tape, but I had no idea how to do it.  It wasn't until I bumped into Richard Houser at our Atari user group that things really started to roll and I began to learn about the system.

I think that I still like the Astrocade so much because of its untapped potential and the fact that it came out so early and gave the user so much power.  Sure, the user was limited to BASIC, but have you ever seen the Atari 2600 version of BASIC?  Yes, I know the limitations of that adored console, but still, it's a pretty pathetic version-- you can't even SAVE!

In about 1996 I discovered Lance Squire's Bally / Astrocade FAQ when using the web; his FAQ showed me how to actually use BASIC because it listed most of the language's commands.  I printed out that FAQ in the lab at school, and I got the "stare" because we were only supposed to print out short documents.  The Astrocade's large tape collection, that most people didn't know much about, and which I had access to (to some extent) through Richard Houser, also made the game library HUGE compared to what the twenty or so cartridges that many people thought that the system had .  Getting all of the very rare information (and especially the newsletters) online to share with other people became a goal of mine, and that's basically how Ballyalley.com was born.

>>
I have no problem with calling, for example, The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (N64, 1998) a classic.
>>

That is a game that my son (who is thirteen now) grew up playing.  I never could get into those N64 Zelda games-- though I really did enjoy watching my son play them.  In fact, I was AMAZED at the graphics of those N64 games.  The reason that I can never get into them is because you have to devote so much TIME to the games like that.  Now, I look at my son playing his Zelda game on the Wii and I can't believe that it is even related to the NES version!  There is a SPEAKER in his controller that makes "clanging" noises and vibrates when he hits an enemy!  I could barely play Brickyard last week on the Astrocade, do you think that I can play a game like THAT?

You keep your variables in an area of the screen that isn't going to be written over by moving objects.  This is usually the bottom of the screen, but not always.  Super Slope is a GREAT example of where you can store your program.  This ML game is loaded using the BASIC cart, so all the program has to be on the screen. RAM was super expensive back then, and this was a way to give you a bit-mapped graphics; you could write anywhere on the screen.  The Atari 2600 has 128 bytes of RAM and you control one screen line at a time.  Of course, the Atari 2600 was so popular that, much later in its life, this software control of the screen was seen as an advantage.

You will find that most code examples that you read for the Astrocade have BASIC wrapped around them in some manner.  This is because for most Astrocade users back in the late nineteen-seventies and early nineteen-eighties, if they wanted to program machine language subroutines, they needed to use BASIC to get the code into memory, and it was also just easier to code most of the program in BASIC.  For many years they didn't even have the luxury of an assembler: everything was programmed, by hand, in pure assembly.  Several years into the Bally Arcade's lifetime there were some alternatives to BASIC, but these didn't come out until much later and they only have a small amount of coverage in the newsletters (mostly just very positive reviews).  These alternatives include: Machine Language Manager (cart, no extra RAM required), Blue Ram Utility (originally on tape but then released via homebrew methods onto cart.  This required extra RAM) and finally there was The General Video Assembler (a tape that also required extra memory).

You will find a brief overview of IM2 interrupts in the "Peek 'N Poke" manual starting on page twenty-one.  This manual is aimed at the BASIC user, but I think that you should be able to gain some information out of it.  The manual is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/peek-n-poke-manual-1-21.PDF

This manual has been retyped, so the text is searchable.  Also, there were numerous typing errors in the original manual (MANY in the programming examples); most (all?) of these errors have been fixed.

Also, ordering a Z-80 Assembly book would be VERY useful to you.  I wrote this list of four Z-80 books five years ago:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/z-80_books.txt

I recommend this book the most out of the four:

Zaks, Rodnay. 1981. HOW TO PROGRAM THE Z80, THIRD EDITION. USA: SYBEX, Inc.

This book includes a whole section on interrupts starting on page 496.

I recently added a complete scan of "How to Progam the Z80" to Ballyalley.com, but I recommend getting the original for ease of reading.  Here is a link to the PDF version:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/z80_docs/Programming%20the%20Z-80%203rd%20Edition%20(1980)(Rodnay%20Zaks)(Sybex).pdf

I just checked Amazon.com, and there are currently fourteen used copies of this book starting at $8.32 (a bargain!).  When you buy the book, make sure that you are getting the third edition (you'll probably need to verify this information with the seller).  Here is the link for the book (it doesn't mention which edition it is):

In order to understand the way that AstroBASIC deals with memory locations I have typed in two programs from the Aradian that have not been archived yet (in fact, very few non-games are archived-- which sort of makes sense). Most type-in games from the early issues of newsletters are Bally BASIC programs and won't work with AstroBASIC without modifications, so try to make sure that whatever program that you choose is from a later issue of the Arcadian (or some other newsletter).  Mike White's software FAQ might help you make a choice:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/Tape_Software.zip

While you can never tell EXACTLY what a program will be like, do your best to choose a GREAT game.

The newsletters are located here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/newsletters.html

If you're really looking for some interesting programs that were possibly never in the newsletters at all, then maybe something here will catch your eye:

You also need a copy of the on board subroutine manual. There are all
sorts of stuff that you can invoke from the on board rom (Gunfight &
etc.) that saves you from trying to re-invent the wheel so to speak.
One of these routines initalizes the screen interrupt for you and
lets you hook other routines into it, such as the music subroutine,
the game timer, and the vector animater. Also, if you decide to
initalize an interrupt by hand you might also want to look at the
origional flag program which was by Barry Ellerson and far advanced
from the simplified one that I presented. It was in THE Z80
MINICOURSE and appears in the Arcadian as well. The only way to get
at the interrupt in the old Bally Basic was to re-initalize. The Z80
MINICOURSE may be archived somewhere (I did send it in).
